newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thailand confident despite Moody's downgrade.
newsitem.headline: Thailand confident despite Moody's downgrade.

text.p: Thailand on Wednesday took issue with Moody's Investors Service's downgrade of the country's long-term debt rating but expressed confidence the economic outlook would improve with measures taken to combat problems.
Although the downgrade would raise the cost of Thai borrowing abroad, the impact would be limited as it had been factored in by the market, central bank and finance ministry officials told Reuters.

"Moreover, there is more than one credit rating agency. I believe foreign financial institutions will look at various agencies' ratings before deciding on the cost," said a senior finance ministry official.

Standard and Poor's Corp last month affirmed Thailand's single-A long term and A-1 short term foreign currency debt ratings, saying the decision reflected the government's substantial financial flexibility.
Moody's said on Wednesday it had downgraded Thai foreign currency ceiling for bonds and bank deposits to A3 from A2.

It said the erosion of the country's credit-worthiness was caused by a buildup of short-term foreign debt, structural problems that affected Thai competitiveness, constraints on the range and effectiveness of macroeconomic policies, and the crisis in the financial and property sectors.
Last month, Thai authorities ordered a revamp of the finance sector and told financial institutions to raise provisioning against poor-quality assets, mainly loans to the depressed property sector.
Siri Ganjareondee, a Bank of Thailand assistant governor, said Moody's should have taken into account measures launched by the government to address economic problems.
"I'm not saying that they were wrong. But I do wish though that they would give more weight to the government's determination in solving problems," he said.
"Thailand should be assessed for its dynamic picture and not the static one."

Siri argued that although the level of Thai short-term debt was considered high, its proportion to long-term obligations had dropped sharply from around 50 percent in 1995 to around 44 percent in 1996.
The positive trend would continue because of central bank measures, which included requiring financial institutions to make seven-percent cash-only reserves on short-term borrowing.
He said a dramatic drop in Thai exports, to 0.2 percent contraction in 1996 from over 20 percent growth in 1995, was more due to cyclical problems than structural ones.
On macroeconomic policies, Siri noted that Thailand did have problems with consistencies between currency and interest rate policies, but plans for adjustment were under way.

"Whenever the situation permits, we will adjust the currency policy and interest rate policy. But in doing that, we must make sure that we will be able to manage the liquidity and the overall economy will not be disturbed," he said.
Thailand floats its interest rates, which are among the highest in the region, but fixes the baht's exchange rate against the dollar.
This discrepancy forced it to rely heavily on monetary policies to cope with an influx of capital seeking high yields and causing external imbalances.
"But we realise the problem and are using more fiscal policy in solving problems now," he said.
The finance ministry official said he was confident the economic outlook would soon improve.

"I think the government has fully realized what kind of problems it is facing. It has done everything that is needed to be done to move Thailand back in the right direction again. But these measures will take time to produce discernible results," he said.
